title: "Ulster Scots"
subtitle: "Ireland"

## Overview

Ulster Scots, also known as the Ulster-Scots people or Scots-Irish, are an ethnic group descended largely from Lowland Scottish and Northern English settlers who moved to Ulster mainly during the 17th century. They are found mostly in the province of Ulster, with communities and historical connections in Northern Ireland, County Donegal, the United States, Canada, and Newfoundland and Labrador. The 1999 Northern Ireland Life and Times Survey found that 2% of Northern Ireland residents claimed to speak Ulster Scots, approximately 30,000 people; the 2021 census recorded 20,930 people able to speak, read, write, and understand it. Ulster Scots is normally considered a dialect or group of dialects of the Scots language. Its folk culture includes language, music, foodways, commemorations, literature, and traditions associated with the Scottish lowlands.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

They identify the Andrew Jackson Cottage in Boneybefore, Carrickfergus, as a traditional Ulster-Scots thatched farmhouse.

### Architecture

The sources identify the traditional Ulster-Scots thatched farmhouse as the building type associated with the Andrew Jackson Cottage and U.S. Rangers Museum in Boneybefore, Carrickfergus. The Maine Ulster-Scots Project has discovered stone foundation layouts in old hay fields bordering Maquoit Bay in Flying Point.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The Maine Ulster-Scots Project is reported to have discovered broken pottery during archaeological excavations.

## Music & performance

Music is identified as one of the traditions brought to Ulster from the Scottish lowlands. The sources state that the origin of country and western music was extensively from Ulster Scots folk music, in addition to English, German, and African-American styles.

The Twelfth of July is associated historically and culturally with Ulster Scots. Marching bands play folk and loyalist songs during events connected with the commemoration. Van Morrison is identified as an Ulster-Scots person recognised for contributions to music. He grew up on Hyndford Street and received music lessons from George Cassidy, a fellow Ulster-Scot and Hyndford Street resident who played the tenor saxophone. Morrison wrote songs about his Ulster routes, including *On Hyndford Street* and *Cyprus Avenue*. The sources also mention the documentary *The Hamely Tongue*, in which filmmaker Deaglán Ó Mocháin traces the origins and present manifestations of Ulster-Scots culture and language.

## Dance & theatre

They describe marching bands, parades, community festivities, musical events, and the documentary *The Hamely Tongue*.

## Festivals & rituals

The Twelfth of July is an Ulster-Scots-associated commemoration with historical and cultural importance. It is a bank holiday in Northern Ireland and in Newfoundland and Labrador, where it is also known as Orangeman’s Day. It is held in the Orange Order in Africa as well. Marching bands perform folk and loyalist songs, while events before the parades include community festivities, learning about Orangeism and Ulster-Scots heritage, different cuisine, and musical events known as “Orangefest.”

The Eleventh Night precedes the parade and symbolises the beacon fires used to guide King William’s ships into Belfast Lough. The sources state that the victories at Derry, the Boyne, and Aughrim in the Williamite war in Ireland are still commemorated by the Orange Order into the 21st century.

## Foodways

The sources describe Northern Irish cuisine as rooted in the staple diet of generations of farming families, especially bread and potatoes. Potato bread, also called *fadge* or *tatie bread*, is a flat bread made with potato, flour, and buttermilk and cooked on a griddle. Soda bread is another griddle bread and is commonly served in an Ulster fry. Wheaten bread is brown bread made with whole wheat flour and baking soda. Veda bread is a small, soft, caramel-coloured malted loaf, while a Belfast bap is a large crusty but soft bread roll traditionally filled with sausages, bacon, and egg. Barmbrack is yeast bread containing sultanas and raisins and associated with Halloween.

The best-known traditional dish in Northern Ireland is the Ulster fry. It is distinguished by griddle breads—soda bread and potato bread—fried or grilled until crisp and golden, with bacon, sausages, an egg, and sometimes tomato and mushrooms. It is usually served with tea and toast. Other savoury foods include Ardglass potted herring, boxty, champ, Irish stew, vegetable broth, dulse, Northern Irish pasties, tobacco onions, Ulster seafood chowder, black pudding, white pudding, and vegetable roll.

Cakes and confectionery include *fifteens*, gravy ring, Paris bun, Florence cake, cream horns, and yellowman. Accompaniments include black butter, a dark spicy spread made from apples, cider, and spices including liquorice. Beverages named by the sources include Bushmills whiskey, brown lemonade, ginger ale, Maine, Punjana tea, Nambarrie tea, Armagh ciders, and Derry Milk.

## Oral tradition & literature

Ulster-Scots literature includes poetry, prose, newspaper commentary, children’s books, and Bible translation. In Ulster Scots-speaking areas there was traditionally considerable demand for Scottish poets, including Alexander Montgomerie, Sir David Lindsay, Allan Ramsay, Robert Burns, James Hogg, and Robert Tannahill. The rhyming weaver poetry tradition produced approximately 60 to 70 volumes between 1750 and 1850. Named Ulster Scots writers include James Campbell, James Orr, Thomas Beggs, David Herbison, Hugh Porter, Andrew McKenzie, W. G. Lyttle, Archibald McIlroy, Adam Lynn, John Stevenson, John Clifford, James Fenton, Michael Longley, and Philip Robinson.

The sources identify works including *The Cherrie and the Slae*, *The Gentle shepherd*, *Random Rhymes frae Cullybackey*, *The Hamely Tongue*, *Wake the Tribe o Dan*, *The Back Streets o the Claw*, *The Man frae the Ministry*, *Alang the Shore*, and *Oul Licht, New Licht*. A Belfast team translated portions of the Bible into Ulster Scots; the Gospel of Luke was published in 2009 by the Ullans Press.

## Language & religion

Ulster Scots, also called Ulster Scotch and *Ullans*, is the dialect of Scots spoken in parts of Ulster, almost exclusively in parts of Northern Ireland and County Donegal. Speakers refer to their vernacular as *Big Scots*, *Scotch*, or *the hamely tongue*. It has been influenced by Hiberno-English, Ulster English, and Ulster Irish. Most Ulster Scots speak Ulster English as a first language.

The majority of linguists treat Ulster Scots as a variety of the Scots language, while some treat it as a dialect of English and others regard it as a language in its own right. The sources describe disagreement over its linguistic status. The Ulster-Scots Language Society was formed in 1992, and the Ulster-Scots Agency promotes the study, conservation, development, and use of Ulster Scots.

Historically, many Ulster Scots were Protestant settlers, and the sources refer to Presbyterian communities, the Church of Ireland, the Protestant Ascendancy, Catholics, Dissenters, the Orange Order, and the United Irishmen.
